e91edd141787.content: MARTIN de ALARCON San Antonio Texas Founder Biography He belonged to a family with a military tradition, which is why in the 1680s he was already in the Spanish army in Flanders and Italy in various campaigns. He also served in North Africa just before being sent to the Viceroyalty of New Spain around 1690. In 1691, Viceroy Count Galve appointed him sergeant major of the Guadalajara militia company, one of the viceroyalty's most important border military posts. Shortly afterward, he was appointed mayor and "war captain" of Jacona and Zamora, both in Michoacán. In the fall of 1696, then-viceroy Juan Ortega y Montáñez promoted him to "war captain" and protector of the Indians of the town of Mazapil. He remained in this position, also serving as an active agent in border pacification, especially in the area surrounding Saltillo. His undeniable reputation and excellent knowledge of dealing with the frontier Indians earned him the appointment on December 9, 1716, by the viceroy Marquis de Valero as commander of the important presidio of San Francisco in the province of Coahuila, as well as the even more important position of governor and captain general of the rapidly expanding frontier province of Texas. In this sense, he was a pioneer in the Spanish policy of territorial expansion to the east, as he was responsible for leading the main effort of conquest, exploitation, and settlement in Texas and Coahuila for more than a decade. While on his way to his new assignment, he had to stop in June 1717 in Saltillo, where, delayed for several months, he attended the investigation that was undertaken against the French Baron of Saint Denis, who, like the Spanish, intended to extend French influence towards the western Gulf of Mexico at the expense of Spanish interests. Saint Denis was one of the architects of the rise in smuggling and the significant increase in the danger posed to the Texas Indians, thanks to the sale of weapons. In April 1718, he was finally able to cross the Rio Grande, finally entering the almost inhospitable and unknown land of Texas: he entered the territory with ten families and seventy-two people. On May 1, 1718, he attended the founding of the San Antonio de Valero mission with Franciscan Father Antonio San Buenaventura y Olivares, and four days later, he founded the nearby presidio of San Antonio de Béjar, which over the decades would become the most important presidio in Texas and its political capital. Most of the families who accompanied him served as the origin of what would become the town of Béjar, a flourishing city over the years. He spent the months of October and November 1718 completing the settlement of old Spanish missions in East Texas, which now bordered French Louisiana far to the east. During these months, he had to combat illegal French smuggling in the area, undoubtedly the Spanish main problem at the time. He returned to San Antonio de Béjar in January 1719 and spent the following months warning the French to withdraw from the East Texas territories, which he considered entirely under Spanish sovereignty. At the end of 1719, his term in Texas ended, and he retired to the viceroyalty's capital. His actions in Texas can be considered the beginning of the true Spanish presence in the region, not only for the founding of San Antonio de Béjar, but primarily for having monitored the eastern border and established a cordon of emission against French interference. The Spanish origin of Texas is therefore closely linked to Alarcón's successful policy.
